title: The Games Xbox Was Built For
blurb: Ten games Microsoft needed to exist for a first console to mean anything: the shooter built to sell hardware nobody had heard of, the racers and role-playing experiment that gave it a personality beyond Halo, and the online showcases that proved Xbox Live wasn't a gimmick.

games.title: Halo: Combat Evolved
games.blurb: The game that proved a first-person shooter could work on a joypad: recharging shields, twin sticks, and vehicles you could jump in and out of mid-firefight. Built to sell a console nobody had heard of yet, and it did exactly that.

games.title: Halo 2
games.blurb: Xbox Live's coming-out party — dual-wielding, a new arsenal, and a midnight-launch frenzy that made online console gaming feel mainstream overnight. The cliffhanger ending was so infamous it became a running joke of its own.

games.title: Fable
games.blurb: Peter Molyneux promised a living world where every choice left a mark, and while the final game trimmed those ambitions down, what shipped was still a charming, quietly moral fable with a genuinely reactive body and reputation system.

games.title: Ninja Gaiden
games.blurb: Tomonobu Itagaki's Xbox exclusive was less a reboot than a statement: brutally difficult, breathtakingly fast, and built to show off exactly what the hardware could do. Still cited as one of the best character-action games ever made.

games.title: Project Gotham Racing
games.blurb: A launch-window racer that turned lap times into style points with its Kudos scoring system, rewarding drifts and clean racing lines as much as finishing first. It set the template Bizarre would refine for the rest of the decade.

games.title: Project Gotham Racing 2
games.blurb: More cities, more cars, and a proper Xbox Live mode that made it one of the console's defining online experiences. The Kudos system got smarter, and the whole thing looked and felt a generation ahead of the original.

games.title: Forza Motorsport
games.blurb: Microsoft's answer to Gran Turismo split the difference between sim and arcade, and added a livery editor that let players paint anything from regimental stripes to full anime characters onto their cars. It became Xbox's other racing pillar.

games.title: Jet Set Radio Future
games.blurb: A cel-shaded skating game about graffiti gangs tagging a stylised Tokyo to a soundtrack of funk, hip-hop and J-pop. Sega's visual style had nowhere else to go after Dreamcast folded, and Xbox exclusivity gave it a proper send-off.

games.title: Crimson Skies: High Road to Revenge
games.blurb: A dieselpunk alternate-1930s America where the Great Depression fractured the country into warring states, told through arcade dogfights in propeller planes bristling with machine guns and rockets. One of Xbox Live's best early multiplayer showcases.

games.title: Panzer Dragoon Orta
games.blurb: A rail shooter of astonishing visual ambition, riding a dragon through crumbling ruins and collapsing skies while the soundtrack swells underneath. Critically adored, commercially ignored, and the last game the Panzer Dragoon team would make.

title: Worlds To Get Lost In
blurb: Xbox never built a first-party RPG tradition the way Nintendo or Sony did, so this chapter is a scrappier mix — a British open world, a Chinese-myth martial-arts epic, and a Dreamcast sequel that only reached English-speaking players because this console existed.

games.title: The Elder Scrolls III: Morrowind
games.blurb: An alien, mushroom-forested island where the game trusted players to wander off the map entirely and figure things out for themselves. The Xbox Game of the Year Edition folded in both expansions and became many players' first taste of Bethesda's open worlds.

games.title: Jade Empire
games.blurb: BioWare's martial-arts RPG swapped swords for kung fu styles you could switch mid-combo, wrapped in a mythic version of ancient China with the studio's usual knack for morally messy companions.

games.title: Shenmue II
games.blurb: Dreamcast's cult classic never made it West in its home format, so Xbox became the console where English-speaking players finally continued Ryo Hazuki's revenge story through the markets and back alleys of Kowloon. Still one of gaming's most obsessively detailed worlds.

games.title: Phantasy Star Online Episode I & II
games.blurb: An online action-RPG that let Xbox players team up across the internet — and, remarkably, cross-play with GameCube owners — to raid sci-fi dungeons for loot. Ambitious for a console still finding its Live legs.

games.title: Sudeki
games.blurb: A British-made attempt at a JRPG-flavoured action RPG, switching between four playable characters and swapping between a bright fantasy world and a darker mirror dimension. Uneven, but a rare console-original RPG built specifically for Xbox.

games.title: The Bard's Tale
games.blurb: A tongue-in-cheek revival that turned the classic dungeon-crawling series into a wisecracking action-RPG, with the mercenary Bard breaking the fourth wall almost as often as he broke into song.

games.title: Champions of Norrath: Realms of EverQuest
games.blurb: A couch co-op dungeon-crawler built from EverQuest's world but designed entirely around console play — drop-in loot runs with a friend on the same TV, years before that became a genre staple again.

title: Live And Let Fire
blurb: Beyond Halo's shadow, Xbox quietly became a genuine shooter platform — mech combat, arena deathmatch, and tactical squad games that used Xbox Live before most consoles had figured out what online play was even for.

games.title: Unreal Championship
games.blurb: An arena shooter built to prove Xbox Live could handle serious competitive play, with Epic tuning the movement and weapons specifically for a gamepad rather than porting the PC game wholesale.

games.title: Unreal Championship 2: The Liandri Conflict
games.blurb: Added melee combat and character classes to the arena-shooter formula, a late-cycle Xbox exclusive built to keep the console's shooter crowd engaged as the 360 loomed.

games.title: MechAssault
games.blurb: Stomping around in BattleTech mechs became one of Xbox Live's first genuine word-of-mouth hits — simple to pick up, chaotic in multiplayer, and one of the games that actually sold people on paying for online play.

games.title: MechAssault 2: Lone Wolf
games.blurb: Added on-foot combat, vehicles beyond mechs, and a beefed-up campaign, though it never quite recaptured the original's lightning-in-a-bottle Live following.

games.title: Brute Force
games.blurb: A squad shooter where players commanded four wildly different commandos — an alien, a beast-like brawler, a soldier and a sniper — switching between them solo or splitting the roster with friends online.

games.title: Counter-Strike
games.blurb: A faithful console port of the PC phenomenon, tactical round-based gunplay that lived or died on economy management and communication. Never quite replicated its PC scene's culture, but a solid entry point for console players.

games.title: Metal Arms: Glitch in the System
games.blurb: A scrappy third-person shooter about a rebel robot fighting a tyrannical toaster army, with genuinely inventive gadget-based combat that punched well above its budget. A cult favorite that never got the sequel it deserved.

games.title: TimeSplitters 2
games.blurb: Made by ex-GoldenEye developers, this time-hopping shooter paired a surprisingly clever campaign with an absurdly deep custom-character and map editor that kept split-screen sessions going for years.

games.title: TimeSplitters: Future Perfect
games.blurb: The series' most polished entry, with a story mode that finally gave the wisecracking chaos some structure without losing any of the mapmaking and character-creation tools fans built entire communities around.

games.title: Full Spectrum Warrior
games.blurb: Originally built as a U.S. Army training tool before being reworked for retail, this squad-command shooter had players positioning fireteams and calling suppressive fire rather than aiming a gun themselves — tense and methodical, unlike almost anything else on the console.

games.title: Tom Clancy's Rainbow Six 3
games.blurb: Brought the series' planning-heavy tactical shooting to consoles with a mission-briefing and breach-and-clear structure that rewarded patience over reflexes, plus a robust Xbox Live co-op and versus suite.

games.title: Black
games.blurb: A shooter built almost entirely around the spectacle of destruction — every wall, car and piece of cover could be blown apart — from the team behind Burnout, applying the same sense of physical impact to gunfights.

title: In The Shadows
blurb: Sam Fisher, Garrett, and a small run of narrative-first thrillers made Xbox an unusually strong home for games about not being seen — patient, atmospheric, and often more interested in tension than spectacle.

games.title: Tom Clancy's Splinter Cell
games.blurb: Sam Fisher's debut leaned hard into Xbox's graphical horsepower for the era — dynamic shadows you could actually hide in, night-vision and thermal goggles, and a slower, more paranoid pace than Metal Gear's theatrics.

games.title: Splinter Cell: Pandora Tomorrow
games.blurb: Added the competitive Spies vs. Mercs multiplayer mode — one side sneaking in first-person, the other hunting in third — an asymmetric idea that felt genuinely new on Xbox Live.

games.title: Splinter Cell: Chaos Theory
games.blurb: Widely regarded as the series peak: a proper two-player co-op campaign built around Xbox Live, alongside a single-player game that finally let players choose between stealth-kills, non-lethal takedowns, and going loud.

games.title: Deus Ex: Invisible War
games.blurb: The sequel to the acclaimed PC immersive-sim arrived on consoles Xbox-first, streamlining its predecessor's density into something more console-friendly while keeping the core idea: every level solvable by stealth, combat, hacking, or talking your way through.

games.title: Thief: Deadly Shadows
games.blurb: Master thief Garrett's console debut kept the series' light-and-sound-based stealth intact while opening up hub-city exploration between missions, one of the few true first-person stealth games Xbox ever got.

games.title: Metal Gear Solid 2: Substance
games.blurb: The only way to play Metal Gear Solid 2 on Xbox came loaded with extra content the original PlayStation 2 release never had — hundreds of bonus VR Missions, a new Snake Tales side-story mode, and a level editor.

games.title: Chronicles of Riddick: Escape from Butcher Bay
games.blurb: A movie tie-in that became one of the best games of its generation almost by accident — a prison-break stealth-shooter with genuinely inventive level design that critics kept insisting people play despite the Vin Diesel branding.

games.title: Second Sight
games.blurb: A psychic-powers stealth-action game about a man waking up in a black-site lab with telekinesis and no memory, telling its story backwards through interleaved flashbacks. Overlooked at release, quietly well-regarded since.

games.title: Beyond Good & Evil
games.blurb: A photojournalist uncovering a government conspiracy on an occupied moon, mixing stealth, combat, and actual camera-based investigative gameplay. A commercial flop that became one of the most beloved cult games of the era, cited by other developers for years afterward.

games.title: Indigo Prophecy
games.blurb: An interactive murder-mystery thriller (released in Europe as Fahrenheit) built almost entirely from quick-time events and branching dialogue, following a man trying to cover up a killing he doesn't remember committing. Wildly ambitious, and just as wildly uneven by its own ending.

title: Crime Sprees And City Streets
blurb: GTA III's success turned crime sprees into their own genre almost overnight, and Xbox got its share of the wave — plus, on San Andreas specifically, a version reviewers at the time actually preferred.

games.title: Grand Theft Auto: Double Pack
games.blurb: GTA III and Vice City bundled together for Xbox owners who'd missed the PlayStation 2 phenomenon the first time round — two open-world crime sprees, one disc, arriving right as the genre they created was about to explode.

games.title: Grand Theft Auto: San Andreas
games.blurb: The biggest GTA yet, and on Xbox specifically, reviewers at the time noted sharper textures, a longer draw distance and shorter load times than the original PlayStation 2 release — a rare case of the console version being the technically stronger one.

games.title: True Crime: Streets of LA
games.blurb: Activision's answer to GTA cast players as a loose-cannon cop free-roaming a recreated Los Angeles, mixing driving and shooting with martial-arts combat. Rough around the edges, but ambitious enough to spawn a sequel.

games.title: Mafia: The City of Lost Heaven
games.blurb: A slower, more deliberate mob story than its open-world contemporaries, set across a meticulously realised 1930s city and built around an actual narrative arc rather than side-mission chaos. The Xbox and PlayStation 2 console ports both arrived two years after the original PC release.

games.title: The Simpsons: Hit & Run
games.blurb: A GTA-style romp through Springfield that nailed the show's humor better than almost any licensed game before or since, with a genuinely funny script and a cast recorded by the show's real voice actors.

games.title: Just Cause
games.blurb: A tropical open world built around a grappling hook and parachute combo that let players base-jump off mountains and hijack vehicles mid-air — pure sandbox spectacle over narrative substance, and one of the last original Xbox releases before the 360 took over.

games.title: Scarface: The World Is Yours
games.blurb: An unofficial sequel to the film that picked up where the movie's ending left off — Tony Montana lives, and rebuilds his empire — with a rage meter and a Little Friend that made every shootout feel appropriately excessive.

games.title: Driv3r
games.blurb: An open-world crime thriller from the makers of Driver, spanning Miami, Nice and Istanbul, with notoriously fiddly on-foot shooting sections that overshadowed some genuinely great driving and one legitimately great single-take chase mission.

title: Full Throttle
blurb: Beyond the flagship racers, Xbox built a genuinely deep bench — rally sims, arcade crash-fests, tuner culture, and Sega's own attempts to chase down Gran Turismo.

games.title: RalliSport Challenge
games.blurb: A rally racer that prized weight transfer and surface physics over arcade forgiveness, with rain, snow and mud all handling distinctly underfoot. A cult favorite among racing purists who'd never touched a Colin McRae game.

games.title: RalliSport Challenge 2
games.blurb: More disciplines beyond point-to-point rally, sharper physics, and one of the better-looking racers on the console — a swan song for the series before DICE moved fully onto Battlefield.

games.title: Midtown Madness 3
games.blurb: An Xbox-exclusive entry in Microsoft's arcade street-racing series, setting free-roaming traffic chaos across recreated Paris and Washington D.C. streets, cops and all.

games.title: OutRun2
games.blurb: Sega's arcade classic reborn with a genuine sense of speed and joy that few racers of the era bothered chasing — sun-drenched coastal roads, a convertible, and a girlfriend clutching the passenger seat. Pure, uncomplicated fun.

games.title: Burnout 3: Takedown
games.blurb: Turned crashing into the actual point of the genre — ramming rivals off the road for boost, then rubbernecking the wreckage in slow motion. Widely considered the high point of the arcade-racer boom of the mid-2000s.

games.title: Need for Speed: Underground
games.blurb: Rebuilt the series around Fast & Furious-style tuner culture — neon underglow, vinyl decals, and drag, drift and circuit racing through a nameless city at night. A genuine commercial phenomenon that reshaped the whole racing genre for years afterward.

games.title: Need for Speed: Underground 2
games.blurb: Opened the tuner formula up into a free-roaming city hub, adding off-road and drift events to the drag-and-circuit mix. Bigger in every way than the original, and just as much of a sales juggernaut.

games.title: Crazy Taxi 3: High Roller
games.blurb: Sega's arcade taxi-driving series got its most content-rich entry on Xbox, adding a nighttime Las Vegas-inspired district to the original two cities, plus a Crazy Box mode full of trick challenges.

games.title: MotoGP
games.blurb: A properly technical motorcycle-racing sim licensed from the real MotoGP championship, demanding careful braking and lean angles rather than arcade forgiveness — a favorite among the console's small but dedicated bike-racing crowd.

games.title: MotoGP 2
games.blurb: Refined the physics and added the full official roster and calendar, becoming the console's definitive two-wheeled racer.

games.title: Sega GT 2002
games.blurb: A GT-style sim racer with a surprisingly deep car-customization and career mode, released into Xbox's launch window as Sega's own answer to the genre Gran Turismo owned on PlayStation.

games.title: Colin McRae Rally 04
games.blurb: The long-running rally sim's Xbox entry leaned into a genuine career structure and damage modeling that punished sloppy driving far more than arcade rivals did.

title: Fists, Blades And Body Slams
blurb: Team Ninja's Dead or Alive series anchored a fighting-game lineup that also picked up console-exclusive guest characters, hip-hop brawlers, and one of Xbox Live's earliest online wrestling experiments.

games.title: Dead or Alive 3
games.blurb: A launch-window showcase built specifically to prove what Xbox hardware could do — destructible multi-tiered stages, fluid counter-based combat, and character models detailed enough that Tecmo happily used them to sell the console on looks alone.

games.title: Dead or Alive Ultimate
games.blurb: A two-disc package bundling a remastered original Dead or Alive with Dead or Alive 2, adding online play to a series that had always been about frame-perfect countering.

games.title: Soulcalibur II
games.blurb: Each console got its own exclusive guest fighter — Xbox players got Spawn, alongside GameCube's Link and PlayStation 2's Heihachi — a rare case of a genuinely platform-specific roster difference worth caring about.

games.title: Def Jam: Fight for NY
games.blurb: A hip-hop-fuelled brawler stacked with a real-world roster of rappers throwing down in subway stations and back alleys, with a create-a-fighter mode deep enough to become the whole point for a lot of players.

games.title: Mortal Kombat: Deadly Alliance
games.blurb: The series' jump to full 3D combat, adding weapon-based stances to every character without losing the gore the franchise was built on.

games.title: Mortal Kombat: Deception
games.blurb: Added a chess-mode and puzzle-mode alongside the core fighting, plus the death-trap-laden arenas the series would keep using for years — a genuine attempt to pad out the package rather than just ship more fatalities.

games.title: Capcom vs. SNK 2: Mark of the Millennium 2001
games.blurb: A dream-match crossover between two rival fighting-game universes, letting players mix and match Street Fighter and King of Fighters casts under a deep 'groove' system that changed each character's mechanics entirely.

games.title: Bloody Roar Extreme
games.blurb: A fighting series built around a simple hook — every character can transform mid-fight into a beast form — that never got the mainstream attention of its peers despite a loyal cult following.

games.title: WWE Raw
games.blurb: An Xbox Live launch title that let wrestling fans take the fight online before almost any other console sports game managed it, part of the handful of titles that made the case for paying for Xbox's online service in the first place.

title: Turn The Lights Off
blurb: A smaller chapter than most, but a distinctive one — Xbox's horror lineup leaned on enhanced ports and director's-cut extras that gave players reasons to pick this console's version over anyone else's.

games.title: Doom 3
games.blurb: A slower, darker reimagining of the original that leaned entirely into atmosphere — flashlight-or-gun tension, sudden monster closets, and corridors so oppressively dark that players fought the game's lighting as much as its demons.

games.title: Project Zero II: Crimson Butterfly (Director's Cut)
games.blurb: Twin sisters exploring an abandoned village armed only with a camera that photographs ghosts to damage them — one of survival horror's most purely unsettling ideas. The Xbox Director's Cut added a first-person mode, a Survival mode, extra difficulty tiers, new costumes, and an alternate ending not in the original release.

games.title: The House of the Dead III
games.blurb: Sega's light-gun horror series translated to a standard controller reasonably well, sending players through a monster-infested mansion with the same over-the-top B-movie energy as the arcade original.

games.title: Silent Hill 2: Restless Dreams
games.blurb: Xbox's version of Silent Hill 2 arrived as an enhanced port bundling in Born from a Wish, a short side-story starring a character glimpsed only briefly in the main game, alongside extra costumes not in the original PlayStation 2 release.

games.title: The Suffering
games.blurb: A death-row inmate's escape from prison becomes a supernatural nightmare full of monsters born from real methods of execution, blending survival horror with third-person shooting and a genuinely grim sense of atmosphere.

games.title: The Thing
games.blurb: An unofficial sequel to John Carpenter's film, built around a trust mechanic where squadmates could panic, turn on each other, or reveal themselves as the shapeshifting alien at the worst possible moment.

title: Jump, Shred, Party
blurb: Xbox never built a Mario-sized platforming icon of its own, but this small chapter of mascots, party games and trick-sports titles shows the console trying — earnestly, sometimes strangely — to find one anyway.

games.title: Psychonauts
games.blurb: Tim Schafer's psychic-summer-camp platformer turned every level into a different character's literal mindscape, packed with the kind of writing and physical-comedy timing platformers rarely bothered with. A commercial disappointment that's been rediscovered and adored ever since.

games.title: Voodoo Vince
games.blurb: A Microsoft-published mascot platformer starring a voodoo doll who could stab, burn and electrocute himself to solve puzzles, since damage done to Vince's own body became his main tool rather than his main threat.

games.title: Blinx: The Time Sweeper
games.blurb: An early attempt at an Xbox mascot, built around a cat janitor who could rewind, fast-forward, pause and record time itself to solve platforming puzzles — a genuinely clever hook buried under stiffer controls than it deserved.

games.title: Amped: Freestyle Snowboarding
games.blurb: One of Xbox's launch-window titles, an early attempt at bringing real trick-based snowboarding culture to consoles with a career mode built around actual mountain resorts rather than abstract levels.

games.title: Conker: Live & Reloaded
games.blurb: A remake of the cult N64 original, rebuilding Conker's Bad Fur Day's absurdly foul-mouthed, movie-referencing slapstick for Xbox and adding an entirely new multiplayer mode built around Xbox Live.

games.title: Whacked!
games.blurb: A cartoonish combat-arena game about D-list reality-TV contestants beating each other up for prize money, notable mostly for shipping bundled with early European Xbox Live starter kits and introducing plenty of players to online console gaming.

title: The Beautifully Strange
blurb: The games that didn't fit anywhere else because nothing else looked or played quite like them — a 40-button mech controller, a deck-building action game, a hero who fights through hell with a destructible sword. This is where Xbox got genuinely weird.

games.title: Otogi: Myth of Demons
games.blurb: A hack-and-slash built around Japanese mythology, with environments that could be destroyed piece by piece and a lone warrior fighting through hell to resurrect the woman he loved. Visually striking in a way few games on the console matched.

games.title: Otogi 2: Immortal Warriors
games.blurb: Traded the original's single hero for a roster of five playable demon-hunters, each with their own combat style, while keeping the same destructible, painterly environments.

games.title: Gunvalkyrie
games.blurb: A jetpack-powered mech shooter with genuinely three-dimensional movement — flying, boosting and grinding across arenas — buried under a punishing difficulty curve and a control scheme few players ever fully mastered. Became a cult curiosity almost immediately.

games.title: Crimson Sea
games.blurb: A sci-fi hack-and-slash pitting a small squad of soldiers against overwhelming alien swarms, closer in spirit to Koei's Dynasty Warriors games than anything else in its genre on Xbox.

games.title: Phantom Dust
games.blurb: A genuinely singular action game where players built decks of psychic-power cards and drew them randomly into battle arenas, mixing third-person combat with deckbuilding years before that combination felt normal. Beloved by the small number of players who found it.

games.title: Steel Battalion
games.blurb: Shipped with its own 40-button, two-joystick controller the size of a keyboard, built to simulate piloting a giant mech in punishing, procedural detail — right down to an eject sequence players had to execute correctly or permanently lose their save file. The single strangest hardware commitment of the generation.

games.title: Advent Rising
games.blurb: An ambitious sci-fi shooter-RPG hybrid meant to launch a planned trilogy, with a script co-written by novelist Orson Scott Card. The game shipped rough and the trilogy never happened, but its ideas and scope still have a following.

games.title: Prince of Persia: The Sands of Time
games.blurb: A time-rewinding platformer-adventure that made acrobatic wall-running and blade-swinging combat feel completely fluid, widely credited with reviving the entire genre after years of clunky 3D platformers. One of the best-reviewed games of its console generation.

games.title: Half-Life 2
games.blurb: Valve's landmark PC shooter arrived on Xbox a year after its original release, physics puzzles, the Gravity Gun and all, running remarkably close to its PC counterpart on console hardware.

games.title: Breakdown
games.blurb: A first-person action game that kept the camera in first-person even during melee combat and cutscenes, an unusual, disorienting choice that made every hit land with unusual physicality. Divisive, ambitious, and like almost nothing else on the console.

title: A Galaxy (And A Few Others) Far, Far Away
blurb: LucasArts treated Xbox as a serious home for Star Wars during this era, and the results — an all-time-great RPG among them — mostly justified the trust.

games.title: Star Wars: Knights of the Old Republic
games.blurb: Set thousands of years before the films, BioWare's Star Wars RPG let players build a Jedi from scratch and walk toward a twist ending still cited as one of gaming's best. Widely considered one of the best Star Wars stories in any medium.

games.title: Star Wars: Knights of the Old Republic II – The Sith Lords
games.blurb: A darker, more philosophically interested sequel developed under a brutal deadline that left parts of the game visibly unfinished — a flawed follow-up that fans have spent two decades restoring with unofficial content patches.

games.title: Star Wars: Republic Commando
games.blurb: A squad-based shooter following a clone-trooper unit rather than a Jedi, with simple voice-commanded squad tactics and a script that made the disposable clones feel like an actual team.

games.title: Star Wars: Battlefront
games.blurb: Large-scale Star Wars battles across iconic film locations, with every playable faction, vehicle and trooper class from the saga so far. A multiplayer favorite that made owning every side of the war feel like the whole point.

games.title: Star Wars: Battlefront II
games.blurb: Added space battles, a proper campaign following the 501st Legion through the prequel and original trilogies, and Jedi as playable heroes — refining nearly everything about the original into the series' most complete entry.

games.title: The Lord of the Rings: The Return of the King
games.blurb: A hack-and-slash built directly from Peter Jackson's films, using licensed footage, voice cast and John Rhys-Davies narration to turn the trilogy's climax into a surprisingly brutal, blood-and-fire action game.

title: The Bottom Of The Toy Box
blurb: Four games that exist because someone, somewhere, was allowed to just try something — a beach-volleyball spin-off, a fast-food advergame, a party game betting on Xbox Live's future, and a Hong Kong demolition derby. Xbox's strangest corners, gathered in one place.

games.title: Dead or Alive Xtreme Beach Volleyball
games.blurb: Spun off the Dead or Alive fighting roster into a beach-volleyball-and-minigames vacation sim with no combat at all, built almost entirely around swimwear customization and physics that became a running punchline of the era.

games.title: Sneak King
games.blurb: A free pack-in game from Burger King starring the unsettling King mascot sneaking up on hungry office workers and construction sites to hand them a sandwich. One of three Xbox advergames sold alongside value meals — the strangest marketing stunt in the console's history.

games.title: Fuzion Frenzy
games.blurb: A Mario Party-style minigame collection built as an Xbox Live-era launch title, betting that four-player chaos on one console could be its own genre. Modest, but genuinely fun in short bursts with a full room.

games.title: Wreckless: The Yakuza Missions
games.blurb: From part of the Crazy Taxi development team, a launch-window arcade driving game about causing as much property destruction as possible across a stylised, neon-lit Hong Kong. All carnage, no consequences, exactly as advertised.
